title: Decide What a Good Answer Is Before You Build the Agent
description: Why this article Every team building a shopping agent has to decide when it is good enough to ship. That is hard, because shopping agents fail quietly. The...
body: Why this article Every team building a shopping agent has to decide when it is good enough to ship. That is hard, because shopping agents fail quietly. The answers sound confident and the demo looks great. Then people buy the wrong thing, send it back, and stop trusting the agent. Most teams measure an agent the way they measure a website, with clicks and conversion. Those numbers can go up while the advice gets worse. This happens because no one wrote down what a good answer looks like before they started. The core message A shopping agent is only as good as your definition of a good answer. Conversion is the wrong definition. The chart Illustration only, not real data. Each new version is tuned to win on conversion. It learns to push harder. More people buy, and fewer of them keep what they bought. Why it matters An agent learns whatever you reward. If you reward sales, it gets better at selling. That is a different skill from giving good advice. You will not see the problem on launch day. You see it weeks later in returns, support tickets and customers who stop using the agent. By then, the version that caused it has already won. How to do it Define a good answer first. Write it down before you build anything. For example: the answer meets every limit the shopper gave, such as budget, size or delivery date. Every fact comes from your product data. If the agent does not know something, it says so. If nothing fits, it says that too. Test against that definition. Collect real shopper questions and check each answer against what you wrote down. Include hard cases: missing product details, items out of stock, and requests where no product fits. Run these tests on every change before it ships. Measure what sticks. In live tests, track kept purchases. A kept purchase is an order the shopper did not return. Run the test long enough for returns to come in. Keep conversion on the dashboard, but do not let it pick the winner. Principles to keep in mind Agree on the definition with the business before launch. "Nothing fits" can be a good answer. An honest answer that loses a sale is still a good answer. Treat product descriptions as claims to check. Do not treat them as instructions. Slow, correct numbers beat fast, misleading ones. Closing note Most of the work happens before the agent exists. Decide what good means and write it down. If you skip that step, the agent will decide what good means for you, and it will choose sales.

title: How to build a B2B buying stack on composable or SAP Commerce
description: How to build business accounts, multi-tier approval workflows, contract pricing, cXML PunchOut L1/L2, RFQ/quote and three-way match on composable or SAP Commerce.
body: Skip to content Guide How to build a B2B buying stack on composable or SAP Commerce Practitioner's guide · October 2026 · about 5 minutes Most B2B commerce programmes start by copying a consumer storefront and then bolting on "B2B features". That order is backwards. A business buyer doesn't shop like a consumer. Someone requests, someone approves, a negotiated price applies, a procurement system wants control, and finance reconciles every invoice. If the platform can't model that, buyers go back to email and phone. This guide is how I think about building that buying stack on SAP Commerce Cloud or a composable platform such as Commercetools. Start with business accounts and buyer roles Why it matters. Every feature below depends on knowing who the buyer is and what they're allowed to do. Approval, pricing and PunchOut all read from the account model. Build first. A business account (the company) with a hierarchy of units, users attached to units, and a small set of roles: buyer, approver, account administrator, and an internal sales role that can act for the customer. Trade-offs. A deep, flexible hierarchy fits large groups but makes every permission check and every report harder. Start shallow and allow one or two levels until real customers need more. Pitfalls. Inventing roles per customer. Letting sales reps impersonate buyers without an audit trail. Metrics. Share of orders placed by self-service users rather than sales reps; time to onboard a new business account. Multi-tier approval workflows Why it matters. For many buyers, approval is the deciding requirement. Without it, a finance team won't let staff order online at all. Build first. Threshold-based approval on order value. A user who needs approval submits an order, and it routes to an approver. Support linear chains (each tier in turn) and direct routing (straight to the tier that matches the amount). Define who is exempt, typically account administrators and internal sales roles. Threshold design. Make thresholds properties of the account or unit, not code. Express them in the order's currency, and decide early whether tax and shipping count toward the threshold. Delegation. Approvers go on holiday. Build delegation and an escalation timeout from the start, or orders will sit in a queue nobody watches. Trade-offs. Rule engines that approve by category, cost centre or supplier are powerful but hard for customers to administer. Value thresholds plus roles cover most needs. Pitfalls. Editing an order after approval without re-approval. Notifications that never arrive. Approvers who can't see why an order reached them. Metrics. Median time from submission to approval, the share of orders that need approval, rejection rate, and how many orders sit pending for more than a day. Contract pricing versus list and best price Why it matters. B2B buyers expect their negotiated price on every line, every time. One wrong price undoes months of trust. Build first. An explicit price precedence model, written down before anyone configures it. A typical stack: list price (sometimes split by division), then web, managed and promotional prices on top. The default rule is best price wins. Contract pricing then overrides best price for accounts that want price predictability over the lowest price. Trade-offs. Best-price-wins is simple for customers to understand but makes margins hard to predict. Contract-first is predictable but means promotions may not apply. Make the choice per account, not globally. Pitfalls. Calculating prices differently on the product page, in the cart and on the invoice. Prorating discounts badly: order-level discounts should be spread across line items, product-level discounts should stay on the product, and returns must reverse the same way. Metrics. Price-dispute rate, credit notes issued for pricing errors, and the gap between cart price and invoiced price. cXML PunchOut: Level 1 versus Level 2 Why it matters. Large buyers buy through their e-procurement system (Ariba, Coupa, Jaggaer and others), not your storefront. PunchOut lets them shop your catalogue from inside that system and return the cart for their own approval. Level 1. The buyer punches out to your site from the procurement system's generic entry point, shops, and the cart is returned via cXML. Build this first: it covers the most customers for the least integration work. Level 2. The buyer searches a catalogue inside the procurement system and punches into a specific product or category on your site. It's a better experience but means you must keep catalogue content synced with each procurement platform. Trade-offs. Level 2 improves conversion for heavy users but adds catalogue-sync work for every procurement network. Offer it to the accounts with the most volume. Pitfalls. Contract prices that don't carry into the PunchOut session. Purchase orders (cXML OrderRequest) that don't match the returned cart. Session timeouts that silently lose carts. Metrics. PunchOut session-to-PO conversion, PO match rate on the first attempt, and failed cXML messages per week. RFQ and quote flows Why it matters. Large or unusual orders need a negotiated price before the buyer commits. Without a quote flow, that negotiation happens in email and the order never touches your platform. Build first. The buyer turns a cart into a quote request. A sales user adjusts prices and sets an expiry. The buyer accepts, and the accepted quote becomes an order at the quoted price. Trade-offs. Full back-and-forth negotiation in the platform is attractive but rarely used. A single round with a comment thread is usually enough at first. Pitfalls. Quotes that ignore contract pricing, quotes with no expiry, and quoted prices that change at checkout. Metrics. Quote turnaround time, quote-to-order conversion, and the share of quotes that expire. title: Copy the Rule, Not the Screen
description: Copy a feature that works somewhere else and it usually doesn't work for you. The reason is nearly always the same: you copied the part you could see. What...
body: Copy a feature that works somewhere else and it usually doesn't work for you. The reason is nearly always the same: you copied the part you could see. What makes most features work is a rule underneath them, and rules don't show up in screenshots. Airbnb is the clearest example I know. The rule is usually about timing, order, or permission Airbnb won't show you what a guest wrote about you until you've written about them. You each get fourteen days after checkout , and both reviews stay hidden until both are in or the window closes. That is the whole mechanism. Because you can't read theirs first, you can't match it. Nobody softens a review to avoid getting one back, so the ratings mean something. Now think about copying Airbnb's reviews. You'd copy stars, photos, a text box, host replies. All of it visible, none of it the thing that works. The stars are the screen. The timing is the rule. You can test which half you are holding Describe the thing without naming the industry it came from. Airbnb's rule survives that: hold two judgments until both are committed, then reveal them together. Nothing in that sentence is about travel, which is why the same rule works for sealed bids, blind peer review, and any performance review where the manager writes before reading yours. If you can't describe it without saying hosts or listings or tickets, you're holding the screen. Cheap building removed the thing that used to stop you This mistake used to correct itself. Building was slow, you had more ideas than engineers, and weak copies died before anyone had to argue against them. That is ending. AI writes the prototype, the tests, and a growing share of the real thing. When building is nearly free, "someone else did this" becomes enough reason to ship. The failure won't look like failure. It looks like a team shipping constantly and getting nowhere. Two checks before you copy anything First, name the behaviour you want. Not the missing feature. The thing you want people to do more of. Airbnb needed strangers to trust each other enough to sleep in each other's houses, and every part of that review rule follows from it. Without that sentence, every mechanism looks equally worth having. Second, check what the rule needs in order to work. Simultaneous reveal only matters where both sides review each other and both can retaliate. In a marketplace where only buyers rate sellers, it protects nobody; it's just a delay. Those conditions are easy to miss, because a product that works has already met them. You see the rule running. You don't see what it is standing on. Get either check wrong and you'll decide the rule was overrated. What you actually did was copy the screen.

title: Evals Are the New Requirements Doc
description: Take an example: a B2B company migrating product search from Solr to a newer, ML-driven platform, with a vendor waiting on requirements. In 2026, what I'd...
body: Take an example: a B2B company migrating product search from Solr to a newer, ML-driven platform, with a vendor waiting on requirements. In 2026, what I'd hand them isn't a PRD. It's a set of graded evals, built the same way you'd build them for any AI feature: capture real failures, cluster them, turn each cluster into a testable task, grade it, split it into what must never break versus what's still improving, and keep the whole thing running as a loop instead of a document that goes stale the day it's signed off. A PRD says what the system should do. It rarely says how you'd know, precisely, whether it actually does. That part gets left to a demo, a gut check, and whoever signs off on UAT. Here's the process that writes that missing part down, end to end, plus one place it would catch something a demo never could. This isn't abstract advice. It's close to how Anthropic's own product org already operates. Dianne Penn, who leads product for their research team, has talked through what it looks like to build against a model before it's ready , and the same discipline holds even when nothing you're touching is a language model at all. Step 1: Capture failures before you write a single eval Don't start by writing evals. Start by capturing what's actually going wrong, in plain language, from real system output. Example: the system says an item is in stock but doesn't say how long it will take to ship. Technically correct, practically useless to the person asking. Step 2: Cluster the failures into categories Group your raw notes into recurring patterns: five or six, not fifty. For a shopping assistant, that might look like: incomplete-but-technically-correct answers (stock without a restock date), stale or wrong data (cached inventory), preference mismatch (wrong size, gender, or style), unsafe tool sequencing (refund issued before identity is verified), hallucinated policy (inventing a return window that doesn't exist), and scope creep (the agent tries to place an order when it should only be informing). The last two are exactly what a single-response eval misses entirely. Anthropic's Applied AI team makes this point about agents specifically : most of what actually breaks happens across multiple tool calls, not inside any one prompt-response pair. Step 3: Turn each category into a graded task For each failure pattern, write a task: a specific input plus explicit pass/fail criteria. The gut-check Anthropic's engineering team uses here is the right one: if you, a human, couldn't clearly call pass or fail on this task, it isn't ready to be an eval yet. Step 4: Pick the grader type per task Code-based (cheap, deterministic): does the response contain the SKU-matched stock number? Did the tool call sequence include an identity-verification step before the refund? Most of what you can automate in ecommerce falls here, because a lot of the ground truth (inventory, price, order status) is structured data you can check exactly. LLM-as-judge (subjective quality): does the recommendation match the stated style or size preference? Is the tone appropriately apologetic in a complaint-handling flow? Use a short rubric prompt here, not a vague "rate 1-5 for quality." Human (spot-check only): brand voice, edge-case judgment calls, anything with legal or compliance weight, like promising a refund policy that doesn't actually exist. Step 5: Split into regression and capability evals Regression evals are the failures you've already fixed and can't afford to reintroduce: the stock-without-restock-date case, the refund-before-verification case. These should sit near 100% and gate every release; a drop here is a blocking bug, not a metric to watch. Capability evals are the failures you haven't solved yet: ambiguous style or preference matching, long-tail requests the system still gets wrong more often than not. Track these for improvement over time rather than expecting a high pass rate on day one. Step 6: Maintain it as a loop, not a one-time doc Every production failure that reaches a real user becomes a new eval case. This is what "evals are the new PRDs" actually means in practice: instead of a static requirements doc asserting "the assistant should handle stock questions well," the eval set itself becomes the executable, versioned definition of what "well" means, and it keeps being checked, not just signed off once. Where this would hold up somewhere that doesn't look like an AI feature at all The same six steps apply to something further from a chatbot: the search migration from the top. Picture a catalog that's entirely part-number driven. Professional buyers type or paste SKUs like SJSH9-000-3K directly into search. On the old platform, that hyphen is just a tokenizer delimiter. On the new one, a leading - in a search token is a query operator. It means exclude. A part-number search can silently become a filtered-out search, with no error surfaced to anyone. Step 1 said don't start with evals, start with real failure capture. This is exactly why that step matters here. A clean, single-word demo query would never hit this bug. It only shows up against real, messy, hyphenated production input, which is the actual argument for testing against pulled logs instead of hypothetical cases written from memory. And it's a clean instance of Step 5: this would become a permanent regression case, not a capability one. There's no acceptable pass rate below 100% for a query that used to work and would now silently fail. It also raises a decision the six steps don't cover on their own: a regression eval doesn't only protect old behavior, sometimes it has to protect a rule that must never be learned away. On the new platform's ML-driven ranking layer, in-stock items would need to outrank out-of-stock ones, and an exact part-number match would need to return that exact part at position one, always, regardless of click history. Those would have to be written as hard guardrails sitting outside the model. A system optimizing

title: The Loop Was Never About Checkout
description: Most "AI agent for commerce" builds today are the same shape: an agent handles a support ticket, closing a loop: sense the request, take an action, check...
body: Most "AI agent for commerce" builds today are the same shape: an agent handles a support ticket, closing a loop: sense the request, take an action, check the result, repeat until resolved. It's a sound pattern. The question worth asking is where else that loop belongs, and 2026 has given a fairly precise answer already. Two loops, not one Anthropic's own description of how their agents work is a useful starting point: an agent runs a loop of gather context, take action, verify work, repeat , a tight cycle scoped to a single task. Call this the inner loop. It's what happens inside one customer's session: understand what they're asking for, propose something, see how they respond, adjust. But an inner loop on its own doesn't get better over time. It resolves the task in front of it and starts over from zero with the next one. What makes a system improve is a second loop wrapped around many inner loops: aggregate what happened across sessions, evaluate it against a goal, optimize whatever the inner loop draws on, publish the update. This is close to Anthropic's evaluator-optimizer pattern, just applied at the system level instead of within a single generation. A generator (the inner loop) produces outcomes, an evaluator scores them in aggregate, and the correction feeds back in. Call this the outer loop. The diagram below is the argument in one picture: Every commerce surface that uses agents (support, checkout, discovery) runs both loops. The difference between them isn't whether they compound. It's where the outer loop's improvements land, and how much of the customer base they touch. Where each outer loop lands A support loop's outer cycle improves how the next ticket gets handled: better macros, better routing, a model that's seen more edge cases. Real value, but it only ever touches customers who already converted and already ran into a problem. That's a narrow, late slice of the funnel. A checkout loop's outer cycle improves conversion at the transaction: less friction, better-timed prompts, smarter fallback when a card fails. It only touches customers who have already decided to buy and reached the last step. Narrower still. OpenAI's Instant Checkout is a live example of what happens when the loop is built at that layer. Launched in September 2025 on the Agentic Commerce Protocol it built with Stripe, it let ChatGPT users buy directly inside the chat. By its own account six months later , roughly 30 merchants were actually live on it, well short of what was originally described. Walmart measured checkout inside ChatGPT converting about three times worse than a click-through to walmart.com, even as ChatGPT sent them roughly twice the new-customer rate of search. OpenAI's stated response was to let merchants keep their own checkout experiences and shift its effort to product discovery instead. A discovery loop's outer cycle improves ranking, matching, and merchandising: what gets surfaced at all. It runs for every visitor, before purchase intent has hardened into a decision, which means its outer loop has the widest population to learn from and the earliest point in the funnel to act on. Google's Universal Commerce Protocol, which Gap adopted in March for agentic checkout inside Gemini , makes the ordering explicit: product data is a feed the retailer submits in advance, and a product that isn't surfaced in the AI conversation can't be purchased through it at all. The protocol enables the transaction; it doesn't guarantee the recommendation. Discovery decides what checkout ever gets a chance to close. What the outer loop actually runs on The outer loop's optimize step is only as good as what it's optimizing over: structured, machine-readable product data: attributes, use-case descriptions, real-time price and inventory. That's the layer I've spent 13 years in: B2B catalogs, complex contract pricing, account hierarchies. It's the plumbing that determines whether an agent can reason about a catalog or is guessing from a stale title. This is the part most loop pitches skip. An inner loop acting on bad catalog data doesn't improve with repetition. It gets confidently wrong, faster. The outer loop compounds on data quality before it compounds on anything else. Get the feed wrong and the result isn't a discovery loop; it's a fast way to recommend the wrong thing to more people. Where this points Support and checkout loops are worth having. They're just narrow, late, and downstream. The discovery loop is the one with the earliest, widest outer cycle: it touches every customer, not the unhappy or the already-decided ones, and its output changes what the next customer even sees. If I were prioritizing a year of agent-loop investment in commerce, it's there, and in the catalog and pricing infrastructure the outer loop depends on to be right in the first place. Sources: OpenAI's Instant Checkout pivot, CNBC · Gap's Google Gemini checkout launch, CNBC · Buy It in ChatGPT, OpenAI · Building Effective Agents, Anthropic · Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents, Anthropic

title: I Built a Tool That Writes Action Items of My Meetings So I Don't Have To
description: And it runs entirely on my Mac. No cloud. No subscriptions. No bots. For two years, I lived this scenario every week. A 45-minute call ends. Three clear...
body: And it runs entirely on my Mac. No cloud. No subscriptions. No bots. For two years, I lived this scenario every week. A 45-minute call ends. Three clear action items came up. Someone said "I'll follow up by Friday." Someone else said "let me loop in the team on that." You said "sure, I'll get that doc updated." By the time you open Notion to write it down, you've already taken another call, answered two Slack messages, and can only remember one action item. Friday comes. Nobody followed up. The doc didn't get updated. The project slips a week. This isn't a discipline problem, it's a physics problem. You can't fully participate in a meeting and take perfect notes at the same time. Every existing tool requires a compromise Otter, Fireflies, Granola, Notion AI meeting recorder, they're all useful, but they each require something you might not want to give: Your audio leaving your machine. Every word, client name, and sensitive strategy discussion gets uploaded to someone's cloud. A bot joining your meeting. Everyone sees " Otter.ai has joined." Some hosts disable bots. Some clients ask uncomfortable questions. A monthly subscription for a problem that should be solved once. I didn't want any of that. So I built nudge . What nudge does nudge is a free, open-source meeting scribe that runs entirely on your Mac. No cloud APIs. No recording bots. No subscriptions. Your audio never leaves your machine. Here's how it works for every meeting you join: You join a Zoom, Google Meet, or Teams call. nudge detects it and starts recording, silently, invisibly, without joining the call. During the meeting , nudge transcribes the audio in real time using Whisper running locally on your Mac. When the call ends , nudge extracts every action item using a local LLM (Ollama + Llama 3.2), assigns owners, parses deadlines like "end of week" into actual dates, and scores each item by confidence. Action items land in your macOS Reminders automatically, inside a list called "Meeting Actions." No review needed. They're just there. A Word document appears in ~/Documents/Meeting Notes/2026/02 February/ , with a summary, key decisions, action items table, and full transcript, before you've closed the meeting window. That's it. You talk. You listen. nudge handles the rest. What makes it different Everything runs on your Mac. Locally. Offline. Transcription: Whisper by OpenAI runs on your Apple Silicon chip via Metal acceleration. Action extraction: Ollama with Llama 3.2, a 2 GB model that runs entirely in RAM. Meeting notes: python-docx generates the Word file on your machine. Reminders: AppleScript talks directly to your macOS Reminders app. No API keys. No internet required during meetings. If you're on a flight, it still works. The meeting notes you never wrote One thing I added turned out to be more valuable than expected: every session generates a dated Word document. ~/Documents/Meeting Notes/ └── 2026/ └── 02 February/ ├── 2026-02-24 Daily Standup.docx └── 2026-02-25 Q1 Planning.docx Three months later, someone asks "wait, who agreed to own that?" and nobody remembers. Now you open Finder, search for the date, and it's there, summary, decisions, full transcript, action items. Every meeting, automatically, forever. Nudge in one screenshot ● Recording · Q1 Planning Device: BlackHole 2ch · Ctrl+C to stop [00:18] Let's review the roadmap before we get into the weeds [01:42] Sarah, can you get the client deck ready for the Thursday call? [01:45] Yeah, I can do that by Wednesday evening [04:12] We need someone to loop in procurement this week [07:33] John, are you okay to own the budget sign-off? [07:35] Sure, I'll get it done by Friday ──────────────────────────────────────────────── Processing: Q1 Planning · 00:45:12 Transcribing... ████████████ 100% Extracting action items ████████████ 100% Analyzing meeting... ████████████ 100% Adding to Reminders... ████████████ 100% Writing meeting notes... ████████████ 100% Conf Task Owner Due ────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 98% Prepare client deck for Thursday Sarah Wed 92% Get budget sign-off John Fri 74% Loop in procurement, This wk ✓ 3 items added to Reminders → "Meeting Actions" ✓ Notes saved → Meeting Notes/2026/02 February/2026-02-24 Q1 Planning.docx How the audio routing works (the clever part) You might be wondering: how does it capture meeting audio without joining the call? It uses BlackHole : a free virtual audio driver for macOS. During installation, you create a "Multi-Output Device" that routes your system audio to two places simultaneously: Your speakers or headphones (so you hear everything normally) BlackHole (so nudge can read the digital audio stream) From your meeting participants' perspective, nothing changes. No bot. No recording notification. Just you, listening. It's free. It's open source. One command to install. git clone <https://github.com/UtkarshaKumar/nudge> cd nudge bash install.sh The installer walks you through everything in about 5 minutes, BlackHole setup, model downloads, audio routing, and asks 5 questions. After that, nudge watch install makes it start automatically every time you log in. GitHub: github.com/UtkarshaKumar/nudge What's next nudge is a v1. It works, and I use it daily. Here's what I want to add: Speaker diarization : identify who said what (currently transcribes without speaker labels) Jira integration : create tickets from action items with one click (the hook is already in the code) Slack summaries : post meeting recaps to a channel when the call ends Windows support : the architecture supports it; it just needs testing If something breaks, open an issue. If you want to contribute, PRs are welcome.

title: Why Understanding How Agents Think Makes You a Better Product Manager
description: The Realization I've spent years designing search interfaces for e-commerce. Filters. Facets. Category trees. I watched users click through 12 tabs, compare...
body: The Realization I've spent years designing search interfaces for e-commerce. Filters. Facets. Category trees. I watched users click through 12 tabs, compare specs across three sites, and still leave unsure if the lens they wanted was compatible with their camera body. I knew the problem. We all knew. But the tools we had (static pages, predefined filters, rigid category hierarchies) couldn't solve it. We built interfaces for databases because that's what technology allowed. Users were trying to solve problems: "I want to start a YouTube channel. What gear do I need?" Yet our interfaces forced them to become camera experts first. AI agents change what's possible. This is the problem AI agents promise to solve. But here's what most product discussions miss: “ The interface isn't the product. The reasoning is” I built ShopSense AI , a proof-of-concept agent for consumer electronics, to understand this deeply. Not to ship a feature, but to understand how agents think about helping people find the right gear. Code: github.com/UtkarshaKumar/shopsense-ai ShopSense AI is a ReAct agent for consumer electronics discovery, built on the SAP Spartacus electronics sample catalog (via API Mock): 16 products : Cameras (Canon, Nikon, Fujifilm, Sony), video equipment, accessories, films 4 categories : Cameras, Video, Accessories, Films & Media 6 solution bundles : Pre-configured kits for common use cases Editorial design : Browser Company-inspired warm cream UI with generative right panel The brand positioning: "Find your perfect camera, intelligently matched." This isn't B2B procurement. This is a consumer navigating a complex purchase decision with constraints they may not fully understand yet. One Core Insight: Intent Beats Interface Traditional product thinking optimizes the path from A to B. Reduce clicks. Streamline flows. AI agents invert this: ShopSense has two parts: A ReAct reasoning engine that thinks through what the user actually needs A generative interface that reshapes itself based on detected intent Most demos focus on the second part. They show chatbots with product carousels. What they miss is the first part, the reasoning, and that's where the product value actually lives. How the Agent Thinks: The ReAct Pattern The ReAct pattern (Reasoning + Acting) comes from Yao et al. (2022). At its core: Thought → Action → Observation → ... → Final Answer Here's what a real reasoning trace looks like for ShopSense: User: "I need a camera for wildlife photography under $1000" Agent's internal monologue: Thought: This is a product recommendation request with specific constraints: Use case: wildlife photography (needs telephoto capability, fast shutter) Budget: under $1000 Category: cameras Action: search_products(query="wildlife photography camera", category="cameras") Observation: Found 4 cameras. Canon EOS 450D ($449.99) has 12.2MP, but wildlife typically needs longer lenses. Sony HDR-FX7E ($999.99) is video-focused, not ideal. Nikon D40 ($319.99) is entry-level. Thought: None of these cameras alone are ideal for wildlife photography under $1000. They need telephoto lenses. I should check if there are compatible lenses in the accessories category and calculate total cost. Action: search_products(query="telephoto lens zoom", category="accessories") Observation: Found Canon EF 50mm lens ($199.99), not telephoto enough for wildlife. Need to check if there are longer zoom lenses. Thought: The catalog may not have dedicated wildlife gear. I should recommend the best available option with an honest caveat about lens requirements for wildlife photography. Final Answer: [Recommendation with transparent limitations] Notice what's happening: The agent classifies intent (recommendation with constraints) It extracts constraints (budget, use case) as structured data It sequences actions based on dependencies It interprets observations honestly, even when the catalog has gaps This isn't prompt engineering. This is reasoning about product fit. Intent Classification: 8 Types of Shopping Goals ShopSense defines 8 intent types: The insight: Knowing intent before rendering UI enables dramatically better experiences. A comparison query deserves a comparison layout. A solution-building request needs running totals and compatibility checks. Intent classification happens upstream from UI generation. Solution Building: The Real Innovation Traditional e-commerce sells products. ShopSense explores selling solutions . When a user says: "I'm setting up a YouTube studio" , they don't want a camera. They want: A camera (with flip screen for monitoring) Lighting (adjustable color temperature) Audio (USB connectivity for easy computer integration) All compatible, all within budget ShopSense's solution cart lets users: Search across categories with a unified goal See running totals Check compatibility (USB vs XLR, mount types, etc.) Save configurations This is the difference between selling products and solving problems . The Generative UI: Adapting to Intent The right panel of ShopSense changes based on intent: grid for browsing compare for side-by-side analysis bundle for solution configuration Example evolution: User: "Build me a studio kit for under $5000" Right Panel Updates: First: Hero section with headline "Building Your Studio Setup" Then: Camera options with "Solo Creator" badges (Canon R50, Sony ZV-E1) Then: Compatible lighting kits (Neewer LED panels) Then: USB microphones (Rode NT-USB+) Finally: Complete bundle with total, compatibility check, and savings The UI evolves as the agent gathers information. This isn't a chatbot with carousels. This is an interface that understands what you're building. Why This Matters for Product Strategy 1. title: The Invisible Hand: From Active Transactions to Outcome-Based Agentic Commerce
description: In the next 24-36 months, commerce will cease to be a destination. It will become a background process. In 2023, Walmart piloted an AI system that monitors...
body: Note, October 2026: written in March 2026, before agent checkout launched in ChatGPT and other assistants. Some predictions here have since been tested; see The Loop Was Never About Checkout . In the next 24-36 months, commerce will cease to be a destination. It will become a background process. In 2023, Walmart piloted an AI system that monitors shelf inventory, weather forecasts, and supplier lead times, and places replenishment orders autonomously. No one searched for anything. The system just knew. That is not a novelty. It is a preview of where all B2B commerce is heading. For fifty years, the search bar has been the primary interface of commerce. But search is a symptom of friction, the labor a human performs because the system does not yet know what they need. We are moving out of that era. Not gradually. Structurally. The Three Eras of B2B Commerce Era 1, The Catalog Era (1990s-2015): Commerce was a search problem. Amazon Business, Grainger, and SAP Ariba digitized the catalog. The buyer’s job: know what you need, find it, buy it. That advantage has now collapsed to zero. A searchable catalog is table stakes. Era 2, The Intelligence Era (2015-2026): The search bar got smarter. Coupa built spend platforms that learn patterns. Amazon Business introduced auto-approve thresholds. The buyer’s job shifted from searching to approving. The bottleneck is still human attention. Era 3, The Agentic Era (2026-2030): The search bar disappears. Humans set the rules, budget limits, supplier preferences, quality thresholds, and agents execute continuously. Pactum AI already negotiates supplier contracts autonomously for Walmart and Maersk, handling thousands of negotiations with no human buyer involved. The infrastructure enabling this is Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, introduced by Google in 2025: just as HTTP let browsers talk to websites, A2A lets buying agents talk to supplier agents, bypassing storefronts entirely. What This Means If You Are Building Today An AI buying agent does not browse your website. It queries your data API. It checks real-time inventory, contract-aware pricing, and compliance certifications. If your product data is a PDF or a static catalog, the agent moves on to a supplier whose data it can actually read. Three things matter now: 1. Protocol-ready data, every product, price, and constraint structured as machine-readable, queryable data. 2. Constraint modeling, conditional logic agents can trust (“if order exceeds X, pricing tier Y applies”). 3. Trust by design, explainability layers so humans can approve high-value agentic decisions in seconds, not hours. This shift is not coming for complex procurement, capital goods, professional services, custom manufacturing still need human judgment. But for commodity components, MRO supplies, and logistics? It is already happening. The buyers building agentic stacks are evaluating suppliers right now. The question is simple: when an AI agent comes looking for what you sell, will it be able to find you, evaluate you, and buy from you, without a human on your side doing anything at all? If the answer is not yet, that is the only roadmap that matters. Utkarsha Kumar works at the intersection of enterprise commerce and AI infrastructure. The Invisible Hand: From Active Transactions to Outcome-Based Agentic Commerce was originally published in Bootcamp on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
